from_notes: In 1638, Shahjahan transferred his capital from Agra to Delhi and laid the foundations of Shahjahanabad.
x: Shah Jahan shifted the capital from Agra to Shahjahanabad (Delhi), founded in 1638.
Abu Talib Kalim (Kaleem) was Shah Jahan's poet laureate (malik-ush-shuara). Qudsi and Munir were other poets of the period.
Abdul Hamid Lahori was the official historian of Shah Jahan and wrote the Padshahnama, not a commander or a noble of Aurangzeb.

x: Shah Jahan's Balkh campaign (1646-47) aimed to set up a friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakhshan, which bordered Kabul; the idea of reconquering Samarqand and Farghana or of a 'scientific line' on the Amu Darya is the tempting but rejected view.

x: Kandahar was the frontier fortress commanding the routes between India, Persia and Central Asia, so its loss was a blow to a strategic stronghold. It was not valued for resources.

from_notes: The mansabdari system, established by Akbar, formed the foundation for both civil and military administration under the Mughals.
x: Not all mansabdars were military officers, and holders of high civil posts were also mansabdars graded the same way, so both are true.
Akbar's mansabdari was modelled on the decimal grading of the Mongol army of Genghis Khan (Central Asia), not on Persia, Turkey or Afghanistan.
The printed key is 'effecting clean administration': mansabdari gave one graded service for army and civil posts. Army recruitment is the tempting option.
source: old app notes 1:133 (old-notes.txt) sub 0 (aim – clean administration)

x: Akbar's military system rested on the mansabdari: mansabdars maintained the cavalry, checked by dagh and chehra.

x: The Mir Bakhshi, head of the military department, ran the mansabdari system (recommendations, musters, pay). The Wazir handled finance and the Sadr religion.
Akbar introduced mansabdari to grade nobles and the army, each officer getting a rank, so I and II are right. Ranks were zat and sawar; chehra is the descriptive roll, so III is wrong.
source: NextGen Indian History APPSC 04 (src/indian-history/nextgen-indian-history-appsc-04.txt) p.32; old app notes 1:133 (old-notes.txt) sub 1-2

x: Mansabdari existed in the Mughal period and mansabs were given at the emperor's will on ability, so the printed key takes both as true; selection on merit does not explain why the system existed.
Mansabdari was Akbar's graded official nobility, so I is true. Mansabs were not hereditary: rank and jagir ended with the holder, so II is false.
Zat fixed status and salary and sawar the horsemen to be kept, so I and II are correct. III is wrong: nobles (umara) were mansabdars of 1,000 zat or above, not 1,000 sawar.
source: old app notes 1:133 (old-notes.txt) sub 1; NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II ch.4

x: The sawar rank could not exceed the zat rank, so statement (c) is not true. The 33 grades in practice, mashrut (conditional) ranks and mansabs for all civil and military officers are correct.
Ahadis were troopers who offered their services singly, were attached to no chief and had the emperor as their colonel, so I, II and III are correct. They were not attached to Mirzas.
Dakhili troops were raised and paid by the state but placed under mansabdars. Walashahi (Balashahi) was the emperor's bodyguard.
The Muhtasib (censor of morals) saw that people lived by the shariat; Aurangzeb appointed them across the empire. Ahadis and Walashahis were troops and mansabdars were ranked officers.

x: The Mir Bakhshi headed the military department under Akbar. The Diwan handled revenue and the Mir Saman the household.
Chakla was a unit between the subah and the pargana but not identical with the sarkar; it was prominent in Bengal under Murshid Quli Khan.
Mauza means a village, not rebellious territory (that was mawas), so this pair is wrong. Khalisa (crown land), inam (grant to learned men) and jagir (in lieu of salary) are correct.

x: Zat (and sawar) ranks were granted and mansabdars fell into three classes, so 1 and 3 hold. Mansabs were not hereditary, so 2 is false; the printed key also treats 4 as false.
Ascending by size: pargana, then sarkar, then suba (province).
Under the Mughals the district was the sarkar; the suba was the province and the pargana the sub-district.
